title: Quantization quality-regret sweep: multi-workload kernels and tradeoffs
body:
Purpose
This doc captures a focused set of experiments comparing quality vs latency/cost tradeoffs across INT8, FP8, GPTQ, and AWQ quantization flows, but with emphasis on the interaction with kernel implementations and realistic multi-workload routing. The goal: surface failure modes and recommend runtime policies (fallbacks, per-route quant profiles, calibration cadence).

Quick TL;DR (read first)
- INT8 gives the best raw throughput and unit cost on short-turn chat workloads, but we measured a small, systematic increase in hallucination rate (~+2–3 percentage points on open-domain QA prompts) compared to baseline FP16.
- AWQ often matches or slightly improves generation perplexity over GPTQ for short contexts, but certain fused kernels introduce a dequant/decode pause that hurts tail latency (p99 +20–40 ms on 13B-class models).
- GPTQ remains the most stable for long-context token fidelity (measured by next-token accuracy on heldout passages) but sometimes loses out in throughput versus AWQ-optimized kernels.
- FP8 is a good middle ground if we accept a ~5% unit-cost increase over INT8; it reduces quality regressions while keeping latency similar to INT8 on kernels that support native fp8 ops.
- Per-layer sensitivity analysis shows attention output & first feed-forward sub-layer are most brittle to 8-bit transforms; a quick policy of keeping those layers in fp16 reduces quality regressions by ~60% with only ~8% throughput loss.

Why this is different from previous quant sweeps
Most of our prior notes focused on microbench latency/throughput across kernels in isolation. This sweep intentionally:
- mixes realistic application workloads (chatty short-turn dialogs, long-document summarization, instruction-type completions) in a single run to capture scheduling contention and cache effects;
- measures end-to-end user-visible quality (QA accuracy, hallucination heuristics, instruction-following A/B test) in addition to perplexity and token-level metrics;
- looks for kernel-level interaction effects (e.g., alignment/padding induced stalls from fused kernels, dequant staging memory thrash) rather than just steady-state raw TFLOPS.

Experimental setup
Models tested:
- LlamaX-13B-v1 (open checkpoint used for internal baseline)
- LlamaX-7B-mini (for high-concurrency runs)
Quant flows tested:
- INT8 (per-channel symmetric quant, static range calibration, no bias correction)
- AWQ (per-row quant with activation-aware scaling, quantizer version 0.9 experimental)
- GPTQ (our standard GPTQ flow with blockwise 128 calibration)
- FP8 (IEEE-ish 8-bit float simulation using our fp8shim kernel)
Kernels / backends:
- fused-attn-lz (our fused attention + dequant path, optimized for AWQ; currently in a feature branch)
- cuBLAS-gemm (baseline cuBLAS matmul path)
- vector-lane (vector-lane optimized pack/gemm path — used for INT8 hotpaths)
Workloads (3 mixes):
- ChatShort: 4–6 turn human/bot dialogues, avg turn length 18 tokens, target latency SLO 120 ms
- LongDoc: single prompt + 1k token generation, target throughput cost focus
- Instr: instruction-following prompts, measuring instruction-adherence and hallucination
Metrics collected (per request and aggregate):
- latency median/p95/p99 (ms)
- tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens (from our internal cost model)
- GPU util, memory allocation churn, kernel launch counts
- QA accuracy on NaturalQuestions-derived subset
- Hallucination-rate heuristic (entity hallucination detected by anchor-checker v2)
- Per-layer activation distribution drift vs fp16 baseline (KL divergence)

Key observations (detailed)
1) Latency tails driven by dequant staging in some fused kernels
- AWQ fused-attn-lz path introduces an extra dequant staging buffer when output quantized format != execution format. In mixed-batch runs we saw p99 increase of 20–40 ms on the 13B model for ChatShort.
- Root cause: the fused kernel schedules a separate CUDA memcpy for the staging buffer on the next CUDA stream to avoid blocking computation; under high concurrency the copy waits for an earlier kernel that had larger temp memory, creating inversion.
- Fix/workaround: two immediate runtime levers — switch AWQ fused kernel to in-place dequant when batch shapes are uniform, or fall back to cuBLAS-gemm path when concurrency > N (N ~= 18 concurrent requests for our GPU profile).

2) INT8: best unit economics, measurable quality regression on open-QA
- On ChatShort, INT8 median latency was ~18% lower than fp16 with cost per token ~30–35% lower.
- However QA accuracy dropped from 72.8% (fp16 baseline) to 69.9% (int8) on our NaturalQuestions subset. Hallucination metric increased by 2.4 pts.
- Per-layer KL analysis points to FFN2 (the second FFN in each block) activation distribution skew leading to saturation in symmetric int8 ranges.
- Mitigation: per-layer mixed precision (keep FFN2 in fp16 or use asymmetric quantization for that layer) recovered ~80% of the lost QA accuracy with only a ~5–9% throughput penalty.

3) AWQ vs GPTQ: quality parity on short contexts, divergence on long contexts
- AWQ tends to preserve perplexity on short completions equal to or slightly better than GPTQ (delta perplexity within ±0.5 on ChatShort).
- On LongDoc, GPTQ had noticeably better next-token accuracy after ~600 tokens — AWQ showed gradual drift attributed to cumulative quantization error in KV cache values.
- Kernel interaction: AWQ fused-attn-lz uses a packed cache format for KV that is faster to write but slightly lossy at 8-bit because of per-row scaling rounding. Over long contexts this accumulates.
- Potential runtime policy: prefer GPTQ for routes where expected generation length > 512 tokens or where preservation of exact token identity is critical (e.g., code/gen usecases).

4) FP8: stable quality, depends heavily on native kernel support
- When kernels natively supported fp8 (fp8shim absent), we saw latency similar to INT8 and quality within 1% of fp16 on most metrics.
- When we emulated fp8 via software shim (extra unpack/pack ops), latency regressed and memory churn increased, erasing the advantage.
- Recommendation: expose fp8-capable kernel feature-flag and route FP8 only when the node advertises native support.

5) Mixed-route and routing policy implications
- Running a mixed workload on a single pool showed interference: AWQ fused kernels produced hotspots in GPU memory allocator that caused transient OOMs for heavy LongDoc requests.
- Policy suggestion: add a simple runtime classifier that tags incoming requests by expected length/quality criticality and pins allocation to a subpool with compatible kernels (e.g., pool-A for AWQ-short-chat, pool-B for GPTQ-long-gen).

Repro steps (how to run locally)
- Checkout branch: serving/quant-sweep-2024 (PR listed in linked_artifacts)
- Run make bench-quant with args: --model llamaX-13b --quant awq,gptq,int8,fp8 --kernel fused-attn-lz,cuBLAS-gemm,vector-lane --mix chatshort,longdoc,instr --concurrency 1..32
- Use dataset: /datasets/quant-sweep/2024/* (NQ-subset, summarization set, instruction set)
- Post-process: scripts/bench-aggregation/quant-agg.py to produce CSVs and compute hallucination heuristics

Open anomalies & discussion points
- We observed a small class of deterministic hallucinations that only appear under INT8 with a particular prompt template (starts-with "Summarize but add minor factual expansions"). Likely a tokenization/quant interaction; needs isolated reproducer.
- AWQ per-row scaling updated in v0.9 causes non-monotonic behavior on rare token sequences; we should coordinate with applied-ml to get updated calibration scripts.
- Kernel scheduling inversion (described above) looks like a CUDA stream priority interaction; SRE should help reproduce with nvprof and check driver-level async behavior.

Immediate action items (owners)
- (Anjali) Add a runtime circuit breaker that routes to cuBLAS-gemm for AWQ when concurrent_requests > 18. (ETA: 2 wks)
- (Miguel) Add a small per-layer mixed-precision rule that keeps FFN2 in fp16 by default for INT8 quant artifacts; test perf impact across 13B/7B. (ETA: 1 week)
- (Priya) Work with applied-ml to produce calibration sets that reduce AWQ KV cache drift for long contexts; try blockwise correction. (ETA: 2 weeks)
- (Ethan/SRE) Reproduce fused kernel staging copy inversion with profiling trace; file a low-level kernel bug if necessary. (ETA: 1 week)

Longer-term ideas
- Automated per-route quant profiles: maintain a small profile DB that maps route -> {preferred quant flow, fallback, per-layer pin list} and evaluate rollout via canary.
- Quantization-aware evals in CI: incorporate hallucination heuristics into nightly regression checks so quant changes are gated.
- Explore a hybrid cache format: keep KV cache in higher precision for layers with high drift while quantizing the rest. Evaluate memory/latency tradeoffs.

Appendix: selected raw numbers (rounded)
- ChatShort median latency (13B): fp16 118 ms | int8 98 ms | awq 104 ms | gptq 107 ms | fp8 101 ms
- ChatShort p99 (13B): fp16 210 ms | int8 172 ms | awq 215 ms | gptq 186 ms | fp8 178 ms
- QA acc (NQ subset): fp16 72.8% | int8 69.9% | awq 72.1% | gptq 72.6% | fp8 72.0%
- LongDoc next-token accuracy @1k: fp16 94.1% | int8 91.8% | awq 90.9% | gptq 93.7% | fp8 93.9%

Notes to reviewer
- This is a working doc; numbers are from runs against a single GPU profile (A100S-80GB) and should be flagged as "node-profile specific". Please help by running a small confirmation sweep on V100/RTX8000 nodes if you have access.
- Major decisions (fallback thresholds, per-layer pin policies) should be validated on Dedicated instances with mixed tenancy to ensure allocator behavior matches hosted env.

References and links
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4213
- JIRA: JIRA-SS-8821 (AWQ fused kernel investigation)
- Confluence: confluence.redwood/profiles/quant-sweep-2024
